emergency.general: Call 112 for police, 113 for ambulance, or 110 for fire. Operators speak Norwegian and English. Emergency services across Norway are well-equipped and responsive, including in remote fjord and mountain areas, though helicopter rescue may be needed in backcountry locations.

healthcare.summary: Complete health & medication guide for traveling to Norway. Emergency number (112/113), pharmacy tips, restricted medications, vaccination requirements, water safety, and travel insurance advice.
healthcare.costForTourists: Norway's public healthcare is funded by taxes and not free for non-EU tourists. Emergency treatment is provided but billed, and costs are high — an ER visit can cost $300+ and hospitalization several thousand dollars per day.
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Comprehensive travel insurance is essential due to Norway's very high healthcare costs. EU/EEA citizens should carry a European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) for reduced-cost access to public healthcare.
healthcare.vaccinationsRecommended: No special vaccinations are required for Norway. Routine vaccinations should be up to date, and tick-borne encephalitis vaccine may be considered if hiking in southern coastal areas during summer.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: Norwegian hospitals are modern and well-equipped with highly trained staff. English is widely spoken by medical professionals. In remote northern areas and on Svalbard, medical facilities are limited and evacuation may be necessary for serious conditions.

medications.prescriptionRules: A valid prescription (ideally from a Norwegian or EEA doctor) is required for prescription medications. EEA prescriptions may be recognized for EU/EEA citizens. Carry all medications in original packaging with a doctor's note.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD stimulant medications (Adderall, Ritalin, Vyvanse)
restrictedMeds.note: Stimulants are controlled substances (narcotics class A/B). Bring original prescription, doctor's letter, and only the amount needed. Declare at customs. May need a permit from the Norwegian Medicines Agency for larger quantities.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine is controlled. Some products may be available with prescription. Carry alternatives if possible.

restrictedMeds.name: Psychotropic medications (diazepam, alprazolam, etc.)
restrictedMeds.note: Benzodiazepines require documentation. Carry a doctor's letter explaining medical necessity.

medications.bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter in English listing all medications with generic names. Keep medications in original packaging. For controlled substances, carry original prescriptions and a note explaining medical necessity. Given Norway's remote areas and expensive healthcare, bring adequate supplies of all medications.
medications.generalAdvice: Norway follows strict EU/EEA regulations on medication imports. Travelers from outside the EEA may bring up to 3 months' supply of prescription medication with a valid prescription or doctor's letter. Carry medications in original packaging with labels clearly showing your name. Narcotic and psychotropic substances require a medical certificate — check the Norwegian Medicines Agency (Legemiddelverket) list before travel.

controlledSubstances.note: Prescription required; travelers from EEA can bring 1 year supply, others up to 3 months with valid prescription/doctor's certificate
Amphetamines are controlled (Category A narcotics) but prescribed for ADHD. Import max 1 week supply without Schengen certificate; longer needs Norwegian Medicines Agency approval
Cannabis is illegal; CBD products with >0.2% THC are banned. Even low-THC CBD may be confiscated. Norway decriminalized personal use in practice but import remains illegal
Controlled stimulant; travelers may bring personal supply with Schengen certificate (if from Schengen country) or prescription + doctor's letter
Prescription required; can import personal supply with valid documentation. Schengen certificate recommended for travel within Schengen area
Available OTC in Norway in limited quantities; travelers can bring personal supply without special documentation
Illegal narcotics under Norwegian drug law; penalties include fines and imprisonment. MDMA research ongoing but not legal for personal use
Prescription opioid; can import personal supply (up to 3 months for non-EEA travelers) with valid prescription
Prescription required; import rules same as benzodiazepines—up to 3 months supply with prescription for non-EEA travelers

scams.name: Cruise Port Overcharging
scams.description: Restaurants near cruise terminals mark up prices significantly when ships dock.
scams.avoidance: Walk a few blocks from the port. Use Rema 1000 or Kiwi groceries.

scams.name: Fake Parking Tickets
scams.description: Scammers place fake tickets with QR codes on rental cars directing payment to fraudulent accounts.
scams.avoidance: Verify tickets through the municipality's official website.

scams.name: Northern Lights Tour Scams
scams.description: Unlicensed operators guarantee aurora sightings and offer no refunds.
scams.avoidance: Book with Visit Norway-listed operators. No one can guarantee auroras.

connectivity.simOptions: Telenor, Telia, or ICE prepaid SIMs at Narvesen kiosks or phone shops. EU roaming doesn't apply (Norway is EEA, not EU — check your plan).
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi at most hotels, cafes, and public buildings. Excellent 4G/5G coverage even in rural areas and along fjords.
connectivity.bestOption: Telenor prepaid SIM for best fjord/rural coverage. eSIM via Airalo works well. Note: Norway uses NOK, not EUR.

cultural.tipping: Not expected — service included. Rounding up is appreciated but never required. Norway is one of the most expensive countries in the world.
cultural.dressCode: Casual and practical. Dress in layers. No specific religious dress codes. 'There's no bad weather, only bad clothing' is the national motto.
cultural.greetings: Handshake with eye contact. Personal space respected. First names used immediately. 'Hei' is the casual greeting.
taboos: Expecting everything to be open on Sundays (many shops closed)
cultural.haggling: Never. Prices are always fixed. Everything is expensive — accept it.

soloFemaleSafety.note: Norway is one of the safest countries globally for solo female travelers, with high gender equality and very low rates of street harassment.

lgbtSafety.note: Norway is one of the most LGBT-friendly countries in the world, with same-sex marriage legal since 2009 and strong anti-discrimination protections.

safety.naturalDisasters: Avalanches and landslides can occur in mountainous areas during winter and spring. Severe winter storms and heavy snowfall may disrupt travel, and rockslides occasionally affect fjord areas.
safety.pettyCrime: Pickpocketing occurs in Oslo, particularly around the central train station, Karl Johans gate, and on public transport during peak tourist season. Keep valuables secure in crowded areas.
safety.violentCrime: Violent crime is very rare in Norway and almost never affects tourists. The country consistently ranks among the safest in the world.
safety.notes: Norway is an exceptionally safe destination with low crime rates and an efficient, trustworthy police force. The main risks are weather-related, particularly for hikers and winter travelers in remote areas. Emergency services are excellent even in remote regions, though response times increase in the far north.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 90 days visa-free (Schengen). UK, EU, Australia, Canada, Japan also visa-free.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: June-August (midnight sun, hiking, fjords). September-March for Northern Lights. May and September for shoulder season value.

stalenessWarnings.message: Some data in this profile may be outdated. Connect to the internet to refresh.

steps: File a police report immediately — get the report number, you will need it
Contact the US Embassy or nearest consulate: Contact the nearest US Embassy
Bring the police report + any ID you have (driver's license, copy of passport)
Apply for an Emergency Passport (usually issued within 1-2 business days)
Notify your travel insurance and airline of the situation
stolenPassport.notes: Keep a digital copy of your passport in cloud storage (Google Photos, iCloud) and email yourself a scan before travel.

steps: Go to the nearest police station (or call 112)
Bring ID or a copy of your passport if available
Request a written report — ask for an English copy or certified translation if needed
Keep the report number safe — required for insurance claims
For theft: list all stolen items with approximate values
policeReport.notes: In many countries, tourist police stations are available in major cities — they have English-speaking staff. Ask your hotel concierge for the nearest tourist police.

steps: If involved in an accident: do not move vehicles if anyone is injured
Call police (112) and ambulance (113) if there are injuries
Exchange contact, license, and insurance details with other parties
Document the scene with photos before moving vehicles
Contact your rental car company's emergency line
Contact your travel insurance's 24h assistance line
roadsideAssistance.notes: Traffic drives on the RIGHT. An International Driving Permit (IDP) is recommended for most foreign licenses. Rental vehicles are available at major airports and cities.

immediate: Check avalanche forecasts (varsom.no) before skiing or hiking in mountain areas
If caught in avalanche: try to grab a tree, use swimming motion to stay on top
Create air pocket in front of face when avalanche stops
Spit to determine which way is down — dig toward the surface
after: Call 112 immediately if others are buried
Do not move injured victims unless immediate life threat
Avalanche rescue is time-critical — survival rate drops after 15 minutes
